Where it began

Mahela Jayawardene was born in Colombo on 27 May 1977 and went to Nalanda College. As a boy he was taken along to a coaching clinic at Nondescripts Cricket Club, and that is where he learned to play. At school he started out as a fast bowler before turning into a top-order batsman, and he captained the college first eleven in 1994.

He joined Sinhalese Sports Club in 1995. It was the ground he loved most, and he would play his last Test there.

The player

His Test debut, against India at Colombo in 1997, came in the match where Sri Lanka made 952 for 6. He chipped in with 66, which is one way to make sure your first Test is never forgotten. He went on to play 149 Tests up to 2014 and made 11,814 runs at 49.85, with 34 hundreds and 50 fifties. He was the first Sri Lankan to pass 10,000 Test runs.

The innings of his life came against South Africa in 2006. He made 374, beating the Sri Lankan record of 340 held by Sanath Jayasuriya, and with his great friend Kumar Sangakkara added 624 for the third wicket, the biggest stand first-class cricket had ever seen. In one-day cricket he made hundreds in both a World Cup semi-final and a World Cup final, and he was part of the side that won the World Twenty20 in 2014.

What made him special

He was a superb fielder, especially in the ring close to the bat, where he was quick to swoop for run-outs. He held 205 Test catches, and the line c Jayawardene b Muralitharan appeared in Test scorecards 77 times.

He was a thoughtful captain, leading Sri Lanka in 38 Tests and winning 18. The ICC named him its captain of the year in 2006, and he led the side to the Asia Cup in 2008. His own bowling was kept mostly for emergencies: six Test wickets, at 51.67 apiece, from a man who began as a schoolboy quick.

Away from the middle

Wisden made him a Cricketer of the Year in 2007, and in 2021 he joined the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame, the third Sri Lankan to do so. With Sangakkara he set off on a charity walk in 2016 from Point Pedro to Dondra Head, 670 kilometres in 28 days, to raise money for hospital care.

He has made a fine coach. He helped England as a batting consultant, then guided Mumbai Indians to IPL titles in 2017, 2019 and 2020. He also served as chairman of Sri Lanka's National Sports Council.

And finally

His partnership with Sangakkara was one of cricket's happiest. They shared records, a dressing room for many years and a long walk the length of the island. Few friendships in sport have produced quite so many runs.
